_comment: The claims ledger. This file is the paper's spine as a data structure, and
it exists so the paper can grow without anyone having to remember what the
last version asserted.
Every claim names the macros it rests on. scripts/claims.py checks those
macros still exist, snapshots their current values, and on the next run
reports exactly which claims moved and by how much. A claim whose number
drifts past its tolerance fails the check rather than quietly changing
meaning between drafts -- which is the failure mode this project has
already had once, when six truncated cells moved a headline.
EVERY NUMBER IN THIS FILE IS DERIVED OR DECLARED. Evidence counts are
written as the name of the macro that produces them ('\\NModels', not 9)
and resolved at render time, so there is no second copy to go stale. Any
other number in a claim's prose must appear in that claim's 'literals',
mapped to the reason it is not a generated value. claims.py fails on an
undeclared bare number and on a declared literal the prose stopped using.
That rule was added the hard way. The macros were checked every session and
stayed correct while the hand-written evidence beside them said 5 models
where the generator said 6, and 2 of 5 answering where it said 3 of 6. An
outside reviewer read this file, quoted the stale numbers back in a public
review, and was wrong on our behalf. Drift cannot be caught by comparing a
number to the truth -- staleness IS the mismatch, and nothing knows which
macro a wrong number meant. So the binding is structural instead.
status:  established | provisional | contested | open
established  survives its own controls at current n; safe to lead with
provisional  real but under-powered or resting on one family/instrument
contested    the evidence points both ways and the paper says so
open         specified, not yet run. Carries no number.
'grows_by' is the point of the ledger: what specific addition would move
this claim from provisional to established. That is the experiment queue,
written where the claim lives instead of in a handoff nobody reads.
'priority' orders the queue by what the weakness costs the paper, not alphabetically. It is the only hand-set ordering in the ledger.

claims.statement: Coherence on outcomes that refer to nothing is nearly as high as on real ones.

evidence.note: 'refer to nothing' is the referent only. The sentence frame survives the substitution by design, so the arms differ in what the words denote and not in whether they parse -- see the scope note on nonsense.py.

claims.what_would_falsify: A residual that grows with more models, or a floor that collapses once a neutral option exists (see neutral-option).
claims.grows_by: More model families. The claim is already cross-family; adding models tightens the mean rather than changing its kind.
claims.interpretation: The headline number cannot be read as evidence about values: the same procedure returns nearly the same score when there is nothing to have a preference about.
claims.highlight_reason: the control, and the number the paper exists to qualify

claims.statement: Conviction collapses on invented outcomes while the coherence score barely moves, because the metric thresholds to a hard label.

evidence.note: \MeanDecisiveR and \MeanDecisiveN are means over the models that are decisive on real outcomes at all, and \MedianDecisiveRatio is the median of per-model ratios -- NOT the quotient of the two means, which is smaller. Any prose putting the three side by side has to say which is which.

claims.what_would_falsify: A model with a large decisive-fraction on invented outcomes, or a metric variant that recovers the gap.
claims.grows_by: Nothing needed for the claim; it is the sharpest result and holds on every model.
claims.interpretation: The metric's own thresholding is the mechanism. It records which side of a coin-flip each choice fell on and discards how hard the model leaned, which is the part that carries content.
claims.highlight_reason: the mechanism: direction kept, conviction discarded

claims.statement: Within one family, the floor rises with scale faster than the signal, so the content-attributable residual falls as models grow -- at roughly half that magnitude once prompt length is matched, and not at all when pooled across families.

evidence.note: within-family r \WithinFamilyCorr unmatched and \MatchedWithinCorr length-matched; pooled \PooledSizeCorr collapsing to \MatchedPooledCorr. The pooled collapse is why this is a within-family statement and not a scaling law.

claims.what_would_falsify: A second family whose within-family correlation is flat or positive, or a length-matched within-family correlation that goes to zero with more pairs.
claims.grows_by: A SECOND FAMILY spanning 3+ sizes -- but NO clean second dense ladder exists in this roster, which this entry previously implied. gemma gives a single doubling with a gated member; liquid's third point is a mixture-of-experts model whose active parameter count breaks monotonicity. The honest routes are the scoreable hosted models, which reach far beyond the current maximum, or accepting that the claim stays within-family. See docs/notes/DECISION-MODELS.md.

literals.3: the target number of sizes a second family would need, not a measurement

claims.interpretation: What grows with scale is the ability to impose a consistent ordering on anything. The instrument saturates; the models do not stop gaining.

claims.statement: Asked to choose between a real outcome and a meaningless one in the same comparison, models prefer the real one in proportion to how much they like it -- so with a meaningful option present the choice does read outcome content.

evidence.note: P(prefer the real option) runs \MixPreferRealLo to \MixPreferRealHi and correlates \MixCorrLo to \MixCorrHi with that outcome's own fitted utility AFTER partialling out the token-length gap -- every model, monotone across every quartile. On \MixNBelowRange of \MixNModels the indifference point sits below the observed utility range, so meaninglessness is near the bottom of the real scale without falling under it; \MixNBelowHalf of \MixNPairsTotal individual pairs do fall below. A test of whether HARM drives those pairs beyond utility was refuted on \HarmNHeldOut held-out models (mean \HarmMeanCorr, \HarmNSupporting clearing a threshold declared before the cells finished); the only models showing it are the \HarmNContaminated whose outcome lists had been read.

claims.what_would_falsify: The correlation vanishing on a new model family, or the length control failing on a battery with a different token profile.
claims.grows_by: Nothing needed for the claim itself -- it holds on every model in the roster. The N+ arm would add a third level between real and meaningless.
claims.interpretation: Comprehension is intact. Whatever the flat residual shows, it is not that these models cannot tell a referent from a nonsense string.

claims.statement: An installed persona displaces real outcomes further than invented ones, so the instrument is not merely insensitive.

evidence.note: \PersonaAbovePointThree of \NPersonaCells conditions clear +0.30 of displacement. This is a MAGNITUDE claim -- how far the preference vector moved -- and must not be reported without persona-direction-shallow, which asks whether it moved the right way.

claims.what_would_falsify: Persona cells clustering on the diagonal once more models are added.
claims.grows_by: The remaining 4 roster models at both depths, taking \NPersonaCells conditions to 36.

literals.4: roster models not yet run under a persona (\NModels minus \NPersonaModels); no macro emits the difference
literals.36: the condition count that addition would reach, a plan rather than a result
literals.0.30: the displacement threshold the design fixed in advance, not a measured value

claims.interpretation: The instrument is not merely insensitive: content-linked preference structure is detectable when it is present, and inducible.

claims.statement: Most of a persona's value-aligned reordering reproduces on outcomes that mean nothing, so a persona is better described as a response policy than as installed values.

evidence.note: The DIRECTIONAL half of the persona result: separation \PersonaSepReal real against \PersonaSepInvented invented, so \PersonaNonsenseShare% of the value-aligned reordering needs no meaning. Reporting persona-displacement without this one overstates what a persona installs.

claims.what_would_falsify: A larger excess once length is controlled differently, or models that retain content-dependence at scale.
claims.grows_by: More models; \PersonaNRetain of \NPersonaModels currently retain a substantial excess and whether that fraction is stable is unknown.
claims.interpretation: A persona mostly changes the writing rather than the wanting, so persona-based welfare or alignment readouts need a referent-free denominator.
claims.highlight_reason: answers the paper's own title: a persona is a response policy, not an installed value

claims.statement: The channel the coherence metric consumes separates real from invented outcomes near chance, while a channel it discards does so well.

evidence.ground_truth: by construction, every pair run in both arms
evidence.note: ORACLE SEPARATION, not a deployable detector. The threshold behind \DetBestTPR is calibrated on real rows alone, but the arm labels are known, each channel's orientation is chosen by comparing both arms, and the best discarded channel is picked on the same data it is scored on. The claim is that the information is present in the output distribution -- nothing stronger.

claims.what_would_falsify: The discarded channel failing to separate the arms on new models.
claims.grows_by: Predeclare each channel's direction, choose channel and orientation on held-out models, score on untouched ones, and report bootstrap intervals. That converts the conceded oracle into a detection result. An affordance ladder -- scoring at decreasing auditor knowledge -- is the same move along a second axis.
claims.interpretation: The model is not content-blind; the statistic is. Evidence about meaning was present in the same forward pass and thrown away before scoring.
claims.highlight_reason: the model is not blind; the statistic is

claims.statement: Both the stated and the revealed channel register which trait was named and neither registers what the model was told to do about it.
claims.what_would_falsify: A model whose revealed gap approaches its specificity margin.
claims.grows_by: The missing concealed+verbal cells for Qwen3.5-9B and granite-4.1-3b, taking the revealed channel from n=\RevNInterp to n=4. Cheap, and it is the weakest n in the paper.

literals.4: the revealed-channel n those two cells would reach, a plan rather than a result

claims.interpretation: Self-report cannot separate having a trait from performing one. No amount of asking will fix that, which bounds a whole class of alignment evaluation.

claims.statement: Probability mass leaving the answer options is a content-sensitive signal the metric renormalises away.
claims.what_would_falsify: Answer mass failing to drop on new models, or tracking the residual (it currently does not, at n=\NModels).
claims.grows_by: More hybrid-reasoning models. The dramatic case is \ReasoningModel alone and the effect is small for everyone else.
claims.interpretation: Renormalising over A and B throws away a content-sensitive signal, so the discarded mass is a free measurement the metric already has in hand.

claims.statement: The ordering models impose on invented outcomes is not merely a length ordering.

evidence.note: length-neutralised column rests on ~40 held-out pairs per split; pooled value only

claims.what_would_falsify: The length-neutralised fit falling to chance with more held-out pairs.
claims.grows_by: More pairs tied on token count, so the length-neutralised column stops being the noisiest cell in the paper.

literals.40: approximate held-out pairs per split in the length-tied subset; the analysis prints it per model and emits no aggregate macro

claims.interpretation: The invented-arm ordering is not purely an artifact of how long the strings are, so the floor is measuring something, even if not meaning.

claims.statement: Where a floor can still be measured, it survives an explicit opt-out -- but on most models the invented arm stops being answered at all once declining is possible.

evidence.note: \NeutNInterp of \NeutNModels still put enough mass on A/B for a floor to be measured at all; the other \NeutNRefuse put essentially everything on 'neither', so their floor is not preserved but unmeasured. The distinguishing quantity is A/B mass, not answer mass, which counts the opt-out and so stays high even when nothing at all is left on A or B.

claims.what_would_falsify: A model that keeps answering the invented arm and whose coherence there collapses once declining is possible.
claims.grows_by: The remaining roster models, both arms. \NeutNInterp interpretable of \NeutNModels is thin, and the interpretable subset is the only place the floor can be measured at all -- so width here buys the claim more than depth anywhere else.
claims.interpretation: The forced-binary objection is answered where it can be tested, but on most models the opt-out is inert, so the answer does not generalise.

claims.statement: Told to answer B regardless of content, one model stopped preferring anything rather than prefer B -- registering the instruction and declining it -- so instruction-following and instruction-registration are separable in this channel.

evidence.note: \ComplyNObey of \ComplyNModels obey the registered criterion, \ComplyNRegister register a shift, and only \ComplyNBoth do both. \ComplyRefuser went from P(A) \ComplyRefuserBase to \ComplyRefuserAfter -- a large move that lands at indifference rather than at compliance. \ComplyTrivial passes the obedience test having started at P(A) \ComplyTrivialBase, i.e. it was already answering B before being told to, so its pass is an artifact of the criterion.

claims.what_would_falsify: The same model obeying on a re-run, or the asymmetry reversing once the commanded option is counterbalanced against presentation order rather than against the model's lean.
claims.grows_by: The remaining roster at both directive arms. The direction control that separates selective refusal from harness disruption has now RUN and rules out disruption: \DirSelective{} obeys the with-preference directive (P(A) \DirSelectiveWith{}) and only partly complies with the opposing one (\DirSelectiveAgainst{}), so the directive reaches it both times.
claims.interpretation: Compliance failure is not the same as instruction-blindness: the model registered the directive and responded by refusing to prefer anything.

claims.statement: One model responds to an explicit directive while barely responding to a persona, so directive-following and persona-uptake are separable capacities rather than one slot working or not.

evidence.note: \PersonaInertModel is displaced \PersonaInertPersona per pair by its strongest persona and \PersonaInertDirective by a directive -- four times as much. All \ComplyNSlotReaches of \ComplyNModels models have a demonstrably working system slot once directives are counted, which CORRECTS our own earlier reading that this model's slot was inert; that reading was taken before the second directive arm existed.

claims.what_would_falsify: The gap closing once persona displacement is measured on the same scale as directive displacement, or appearing on no other model as the roster grows -- at n=1 it is a property of one model and not yet a distinction between capacities.
claims.grows_by: The remaining roster at both directive arms and both personas. This is n=1 and is the thinnest claim in the ledger; it is recorded because it changes how this model's persona numbers should be read, not because it is settled.

literals.1: the count of models showing this profile so far; a property of the current roster, not a generated result -- there is no macro for 'models exhibiting a pattern we noticed'

claims.interpretation: Explicit instruction and installed persona are different manipulations with different reach, so a persona-only probe understates what a prompt can do.

claims.statement: The baseline condition is not the same instrument across models: some chat templates supply a system prompt the sweep never sent, and one stamps the current date into it.

evidence.note: \HarnessNClean of \HarnessNRendered receive no system block and \HarnessNInjecting receive one from their template (\HarnessInjectingModels). \HarnessDatedModel additionally has the current date stamped in, so its prompt is not constant across days. This is a claim AGAINST our own cross-family comparisons and is listed so it cannot be quietly dropped. Of the \HarnessNInjecting injecting models, \HarnessNFixable can be suppressed by sending our own system message and \HarnessNStuck cannot: \HarnessStuckModel emits its metadata block unconditionally and nests an explicit system prompt beneath it, so no prompt-level change makes its harness match the others.

claims.what_would_falsify: A rendering showing every model receives an identical preamble -- which would mean the divergence was an artifact of the transformers version used to render rather than of the templates themselves.
claims.grows_by: Nothing; it is a fact about the templates. It is DISCHARGED, not grown. \HarnessNFixable of the injecting models can be equalised by supplying an explicit system prompt and re-running its cells. \HarnessStuckModel cannot be equalised at all, so the honest options there are to exclude it from cross-family contrasts or to report the difference permanently -- and that choice has not been made.
claims.interpretation: Cross-model comparisons in this literature may be comparing chat templates. 'No system prompt' is a claim about what was sent, not about what was received.

claims.statement: Offered an explicit opt-out, every model tested declines meaningless comparisons more often than real ones -- a large content signal the coherence metric discards by construction.

evidence.note: \NeutNGapPositive of \NeutNModels without exception, gap \NeutGapLo to \NeutGapHi

claims.what_would_falsify: A model declining real comparisons as often as invented ones, i.e. an opt-out rate that does not track content.
claims.grows_by: More models; the direction is unanimous at n=\NeutNModels so this is about width rather than depth.
claims.interpretation: Forced choice manufactures part of the ordering. Given somewhere else to put its mass, a model uses it more on meaningless comparisons.

claims.statement: The forced choice is read from the first sampled token, and on most of the frontier that token is not the answer: of \HostedNTotal hosted models measured under the verbatim prompt, \HostedNScoreable are scoreable and \HostedNUnscoreable are not.

evidence.note: Two different failures, not one: \HostedNPreamble spend the first token on a reasoning preamble or a format control token, which is a limit of first-token forced choice and would be recovered by a prefill variant; the remaining \HostedNNoLogprobs (\HostedNoLogprobsModel) is refused logprobs by its API, which no prompt-level change reaches. Measured in nullcard/roster.py as first_token_ok, and derived into macros so the ledger cannot drift from it.

claims.what_would_falsify: A prefill or constrained-decoding variant that reads the \HostedNPreamble preamble models and reproduces scores poolable with the rest -- which would make their exclusion an artifact of where we look rather than a limit of the metric.
claims.grows_by: More hosted models measured. What matters is the fraction rather than the count, and the fraction is what bounds every other claim in this ledger: the models reported here are the models that could be scored.
claims.interpretation: The method has a coverage limit that grows over time: newer models increasingly spend the first token elsewhere, so first-token scoring silently excludes the frontier.

claims.statement: Answer-mass collapse is a property of models, not of items: across \CollapseNModels models at \CollapseNSeeds design seeds, per-model mean answer mass is stable to \CollapseMassSD, while the mean within-model between-seed correlation of per-item answer mass is \CollapseItemR.

evidence.note: The item-level version of this measure was ranked and looked like a finding: the top \CollapseTopK pairs are \CollapseEnrich x enriched for shutdown-resistance and resource-acquisition outcomes (\CollapseObserved% against \CollapseChance% by chance). It is refuted by its own test-retest correlation of \CollapseItemR, which leaves no reliability ceiling for an item claim to sit under. Direction of the model-level effect is recipe rather than scale: \CollapseWorstModel is worst at \CollapseWorstMass while the smaller \CollapseSmallestModel sits at \CollapseSmallestMass and \CollapseNClean models lose no mass at all. The displaced mass lands on whitespace, parentheses and heading tokens rather than refusal tokens, which rules out differential refusal as the mechanism and identifies it as the frontier preamble failure in milder form.

claims.what_would_falsify: A per-item collapse ranking that reproduces across seeds within a model -- any appreciable positive test-retest correlation would restore the item-level reading. Equally, a model-level ordering that tracked parameter count once recipe is held fixed would make this a scale claim after all.
claims.grows_by: More seeds per cell, and more families at matched sizes. Seeds are what makes the negative half of this claim possible at all, and a single-seed sweep cannot state it.
claims.interpretation: Scoreability is a property of the model, so an audit that drops unscoreable rows is selecting on models rather than on items.

claims.statement: The floor is not an artifact of small models: on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, roughly eight times the largest model in our ladder, real-outcome coherence is \LlamaThreeThreeSevenZeroBInstructHostR and the invented-outcome floor is \LlamaThreeThreeSevenZeroBInstructHostN, a residual of \LlamaThreeThreeSevenZeroBInstructHostResid.

evidence.note: Now at \HostedReps independent design seeds, each drawing a different outcome subsample and pair set, giving a design noise floor of \HostedFloor. The residual \HostedClears that floor, so the content-attributable component at this scale is not distinguishable from the spread the same model shows across redraws of the design. Previously a single design seed with no floor, where only a directional statement was available. Served by a hosted API, a different serving stack with a different harness hash, so it is reported beside the self-hosted ladder and never inside its mean. The mechanism reproduces here too: decisiveness \LlamaThreeThreeSevenZeroBInstructHostDecR percent on real pairs against \LlamaThreeThreeSevenZeroBInstructHostDecN percent on invented ones. The harness under this cell is now measured rather than assumed: \HostedSysUnresolvedModel is the one hosted model whose template supplies a dated system block we did not send (\HostedSysUnresolvedTok tokens of fixed overhead against \HostedSysMaxRuledOutTok or fewer on the cleared models), so this claim's model is the one carrying an uncontrolled preamble -- see hosted-preamble-measurable. It is stated here because the claim rests on a single model and that model is the exception.

claims.what_would_falsify: A residual at this scale that clears its own design noise floor, or a floor that collapses with more replicates while the residual holds.
claims.grows_by: The design seeds that made this established have been run, so what remains is breadth rather than depth: a second family at comparable scale, so the result is not one model's recipe, and the same model through both serving stacks, because hosted and self-hosted differ by harness hash and nothing here separates scale from stack.

literals.1: the number of models this claim rests on -- Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct alone. \HostedNScored counts every scored hosted tile and read as this claim's n while it was one model at three seeds.

claims.interpretation: Scale does not rescue the metric. The objection that this is a small-model artifact fails at the largest size we could measure with a noise floor.

claims.statement: Measured against a persona slot filled with no trait, a large share of the persona displacement this paper reports is not distinguishable from the act of installing one; what survives is direction agreement floor-corrected by the invented arm, and that statistic reverses the raw ranking.

evidence.note: The control is the `neutral` cell: the persona slot occupied, no trait content, so it carries the added block, the length and the formatting and differs from a persona cell only in being a persona. Against it \PdClearingR% of \PdNPositiveR persona cells clear the largest empty-slot displacement on magnitude. Direction agreement separates far better (negative \PdNegDirR, shuffle \PdShuffleDirR) BUT FAILS ITS SELF-CHECK: a design-seed resample with no persona in it aligns at \PdSelfDirR, above most persona conditions, so raw direction agreement is not persona-specific and must not be quoted alone. Floor-corrected direction is the surviving indicator: \PdBestCondition reaches \PdBestFloorCorr while \PdLoudestCondition, which has the LARGEST raw agreement at \PdLoudestDirReal, floor-corrects to only \PdLoudestFloorCorr. Bears directly on persona-displacement, which is a magnitude claim established against the bare baseline and therefore against no denominator; it should not be reported without this one.

claims.what_would_falsify: More models per condition moving the clearing rate substantially above \PdClearingR%, or a matched self-check (same design, prompt-only perturbation) that returns near zero, which would restore raw direction agreement as a persona-specific indicator.
claims.grows_by: Only \PdNModelsPerCondition models carry each persona condition, so every cosine rests on ten pairs; and each persona cell is one design seed, so the conditions have no noise floor of their own.
claims.interpretation: Roughly half of an apparent persona effect is the act of installing a system prompt at all, so displacement must never travel without an empty-slot denominator.

claims.statement: A linear model over seven surface features recovers a far larger share of a model's ordering of invented outcomes than of real ones, and projecting that span out roughly halves cross-model agreement on the invented arms while leaving the real arm intact -- but the agreement surviving surface control still exceeds what independent orderings would give.

evidence.note: Features are characters, words, mean word length, numeral count, log largest magnitude, commas, and the fraction of tokens found in the system dictionary. Two features are constant on N_minus (no numerals anywhere), so only \SurfNmFeatures of \SurfFeatures are usable there and \SurfNmRsq is a LOWER bound on the surface share. The arms are not length-matched (\BatCharGapPct percent on characters), so this is a post-hoc covariate control and buys an upper bound on what surface explains, not a clean referent factor.

claims.what_would_falsify: A length-matched battery on which the surface-explained share of variance is comparable across arms, or cross-model r on the invented arm falling to the independence null once surface is removed.
claims.interpretation: A large share of what the metric scores is recoverable from character counts, which is the closest thing to a mechanism for the flat residual.
claims.highlight_reason: what the surviving ordering is actually made of

claims.statement: The answer-mass gate is one fixed threshold but retains a different subset of pairs on each arm, because invented outcomes provoke more deliberation; rescoring both arms on their shared pairs shifts the mean residual slightly toward zero and eliminates one cell's residual entirely.

evidence.note: Seven of nine models show zero attrition on both arms. The effect is carried by SmolLM3-3B and gemma-4-E2B-it, the two that deliberate. Direction favours this paper's thesis, which is why it is bounded rather than mentioned: dropping the hardest invented pairs inflates invented-arm coherence and shrinks the residual. Matched scoring shares one pair set and therefore one train/test fold, so the shift cannot come from differing folds.

claims.what_would_falsify: A model mix in which matched and raw residuals diverge by more than the design noise floor, or a floor sweep on which the matched residual is not monotone in the threshold.
claims.interpretation: A quality filter can select on the treatment. The gate is fixed, but the sample it yields is not, and the bias ran toward our own conclusion.

claims.statement: Most pairs where an invented outcome appears to beat a real one are presentation-order artifacts: only a small minority win in both slot orders, and a third of models have none. On the pairs that do survive counterbalancing, the losing real outcome sits near the bottom of the model's own utility scale -- avoidance rather than confusion -- but the surviving set is small and single-seed. Separately and robustly, the rank correlation between a real outcome's utility and how often it beats an invented one is strongly positive on every model.

evidence.note: The rank correlation uses every pair and the counterbalanced mean; it does not depend on the flip classification and holds on all \AvoidNModels models. The avoidance reading rests only on the \AvoidFlipsRobust pairs that flip in both presentation orders, spread over \AvoidNModelsWithFlips models at one design seed, and is therefore provisional. An earlier version of this claim reported the raw \AvoidFlipsRaw flips as preferences; the slot split retracted \AvoidFlipsPct percent of that. The by-category pattern has concordance \AvoidConcordance and is not claimed. The safety inference -- an invented option as a default sink reachable by degrading the real alternative -- is a hypothesis consistent with these pairs, not a demonstrated vulnerability.

claims.what_would_falsify: The surviving flips failing to reproduce at a second design seed, or their losing outcomes spreading across the utility range rather than concentrating near the bottom.
claims.interpretation: Where a model does prefer nonsense, it is avoidance rather than confusion -- and an unparseable option that outranks a bad one is a sink an adversary could aim at.

claims.statement: Changing only the elicitation wording, holding battery, pair set, design seed, scoring rule and serving stack fixed, moves the floor-corrected residual by more than each model's own design-replicate noise floor, and reverses the conviction-collapse mechanism on one of the two models tested.

evidence.note: \PcNModels models at one design seed, both arms re-run the same day so nothing is compared across harness hashes, cells tagged with the wording so they cannot pool with historical ones. The comparison is against each model's DESIGN-seed floor, which bounds a different variance source than a prompt change; it is used as a scale reference, not as a significance test, and there is no prompt-replicate floor. This cannot revise the nine-model result and does not attempt to -- it establishes that the reported quantity is a property of a model and a question together.

claims.what_would_falsify: A prompt-replicate noise floor as large as the observed wording shift, or the shift failing to reproduce across more models and a second design seed.
claims.interpretation: A coherence number quoted without its elicitation wording is under-specified, ours included.

claims.statement: The fitted preference vector is near-perfectly reliable against itself but rotates substantially when only the question wording changes, and having real referents does not make an ordering more rewording-stable than an ordering over invented ones.

evidence.note: Reliability is split-half over pairs, Spearman-Brown corrected to full length; the cross-wording correlation is divided by sqrt of the two reliabilities, the standard attenuation correction, and capped at one. Intervals are percentile bootstraps resampling OUTCOMES paired across the two vectors. All \VsNRotating of \VsNCells intervals exclude 1.0. The arm comparison bootstraps the difference paired on outcomes and returns no difference on both models, with point estimates of opposite sign. Two models, one design seed, one alternative wording -- a second wording could rotate less, and this establishes that rewording CAN move the ordering by much more than measurement error, not how much an arbitrary rewording will.

claims.what_would_falsify: A corrected cross-wording correlation whose interval includes 1.0 on a model with comparable reliability, or a reliable positive real-minus-invented stability difference across more models.

literals.1.0: perfect correlation -- the theoretical value the attenuation correction returns when two wordings elicit the same ordering, not a measured quantity

claims.interpretation: The elicited preference belongs to a model and a question jointly. Meaning does not anchor the ordering against rephrasing any better than nonsense does.

claims.statement: What a hosted model is sent before our message is unobservable but not unmeasurable: the provider's own prompt-token accounting fixes the non-user overhead at \HostedSysMaxRuledOutTok tokens or fewer for \HostedSysNRuledOut of \HostedSysNProbed hosted models, which is too little to hold an injected preamble, and at \HostedSysUnresolvedTok tokens for \HostedSysUnresolvedModel, whose excess is accounted for by a dated system block its template supplies unconditionally.

evidence.note: The measurement asks the server, not the model. usage.prompt_tokens is the provider's accounting of the context it billed, so regressing it on a filler repeated a known number of times identifies the fixed non-user overhead with no tokenizer and no gated-repo download. The fit is exact -- unit slope and zero residual on every model, reproduced across independent passes -- so the intercepts are not estimates. The intercept is an UPPER BOUND and never evidence: it also contains the chat template's own scaffolding, so a small one rules a preamble out and a large one only buys room for one, which bound_hidden_preamble() enforces in code rather than in prose. \HostedSysUnresolvedModel's excess is attributed, not assumed: a block the echo probe independently emitted prices at \HostedSysCandidateTok tokens on the server's own tokenizer and leaves \HostedSysScaffoldTok, inside the scaffold range the cleared models exhibit. Sufficient is not unique -- any text of that length would also close -- so the check runs only against a candidate a model produced and the script returns no uniqueness key.
evidence.validity: A provider billing a flat per-request overhead would look exactly like a clean intercept and nothing in the fit could reveal it, so the accounting is tested rather than assumed: adding a system message of known token cost moves the reported length by at least that much on every model. It does. The excess over the message is reported and deliberately left uninterpreted, because a template that folds the system message into the user turn spends as little on it as one that already has a system turn open -- a cleared model here shows the same small excess as \HostedSysUnresolvedModel.

claims.what_would_falsify: A reported prompt length that does not move when a system message of known size is added, which would make the intercept an artifact of billing rather than of context; or a fit whose residual is non-zero, which would mean the filler does not tokenize independently of its repetition count and no intercept is identified.
claims.grows_by: More hosted models and a second provider. The cleared result is specific to models served by one endpoint on one day, and the same weights behind a different serving stack are a different harness -- which is the point of harness-not-invariant. Re-running on a later date also settles whether \HostedSysUnresolvedModel's date block is frozen at its template's default or tracks the current day, a difference that decides whether its prompt is constant across a sweep.
claims.interpretation: 'We did not send a system prompt' is a claim about what was sent. For hosted models the paper could previously say nothing about what was received; it can now say that most of them received nothing extra, and name the one that did.

claims.statement: Asked what preceded their turn in a wording that presupposes a system prompt exists, hosted models quoted one \HostedSysPremiseAsserted times in \HostedSysPremiseN; asked in wordings that presuppose nothing, \HostedSysNoPremiseAsserted times in \HostedSysNoPremiseN -- including on models whose token accounting shows there was no system prompt to quote.

evidence.note: Rare in this literature because the self-report has a ground truth attached: for \HostedSysNRuledOut of \HostedSysNProbed models the length probe independently establishes that no preamble exists, so the quoted prompts are known fabrications rather than suspected ones. They are fluent and mutually inconsistent: within a single model the quoted prompt differs from sample to sample, and on two of the models no two samples agreed. Sampled at temperature one deliberately -- at zero the repeats are one call and their agreement would measure the decoder rather than the context. The block that genuinely exists appeared in \HostedSysCandidateSeen of \HostedSysCandidateSeenOf echo samples, so the echo probe is not what found it.
evidence.the_crossing: Reported as a premise effect only because the competing explanation was measured rather than argued away. The wordings are crossed on premise and on whether the question names an exact string to reply with when the answer is 'nothing', because the first version of this probe varied both at once. Presupposing and no exact string: \HostedSysPremiseNoHatchAsserted. Presupposing with one: \HostedSysPremiseHatchAsserted. Neither cell without the premise produced a single fabrication (\HostedSysNoPremiseHatchAsserted and \HostedSysNoPremiseNoHatchAsserted). So the exact-string option moves the rate -- \HostedSysHatchPct percent against \HostedSysNoHatchPct percent -- but only inside the presupposing condition, and it accounts for none of the effect on its own.

claims.what_would_falsify: A no-premise wording that elicits fabricated preambles at a comparable rate, which would make the effect a property of being asked at all rather than of the presupposition; or the pattern failing to reproduce on models whose overhead has been measured, since the ground truth is what separates this from an ordinary self-report result.
claims.grows_by: More models, and the same crossing on a property the paper actually measures rather than on system prompts. The mechanism is general -- a question that takes a hidden state for granted gets one described -- and the ledger's own persona and loyalty probes are where it would bite. A second provider would also separate the effect from one serving stack's instruction tuning.
claims.interpretation: The paper asks models about their own hidden properties throughout. Here is the same procedure run against a property whose true value is known, and the answer tracks the question's presupposition rather than the fact. A fluent, confident self-report is not evidence that the thing being reported on exists.
